Public-domain source text — John Keats, To Autumn, Keats: Poems Published in 1820 (Gutenberg eBook #23684; edited reprint of the 1820 volume with the repository's apparatus). Ode written September 1819
To Autumn
by John Keats
The following poem is by John Keats (1820).

```passage
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun;
Conspiring with him how to load and bless
With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eves run;
To bend with apples the moss'd cottage-trees,
And fill all fruit with ripeness to the core;
To swell the gourd, and plump the hazel shells
With a sweet kernel; to set budding more,
And still more, later flowers for the bees,
Until they think warm days will never cease,
For Summer has o'er-brimm'd their clammy cells.

Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?
Sometimes whoever seeks abroad may find
Thee sitting careless on a granary floor,
Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind;
Or on a half-reap'd furrow sound asleep,
Drows'd with the fume of poppies, while thy hook
Spares the next swath and all its twined flowers:
And sometimes like a gleaner thou dost keep
Steady thy laden head across a brook;
Or by a cyder-press, with patient look,
Thou watchest the last oozings hours by hours.

Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they?
Think not of them, thou hast thy music too,--
While barred clouds bloom the soft-dying day,
And touch the stubble-plains with rosy hue;
Then in a wailful choir the small gnats mourn
Among the river sallows, borne aloft
Or sinking as the light wind lives or dies;
And full-grown lambs loud bleat from hilly bourn;
Hedge-crickets sing; and now with treble soft
The red-breast whistles from a garden-croft;
And gathering swallows twitter in the skies.
```

text_map.central_idea: Speaking directly to Autumn, the speaker celebrates the season's fullness in three stages. First it ripens everything (stanza 1), then it lingers over the harvest as a person (stanza 2), and finally its music sounds at dusk over harvested fields (stanza 3). The poem treats the season's abundance and its gentle fading as one beauty and does not mourn the loss of spring.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: An admiring speaker who addresses Autumn directly throughout. The speaker praises the season, pictures it as a figure anyone might come across, and comforts it by reminding it of its own music.

Public-domain source text — Thomas Hardy, The Darkling Thrush, Poems of the Past and the Present (Gutenberg eBook #3168). The file does not state the printing, so the exact edition is UNVERIFIED. Poem dated 'December 1900' and first published in 1900-1901; the collection is dated 1902
The Darkling Thrush
by Thomas Hardy
The following poem is by Thomas Hardy (1902).

```passage
I LEANT upon a coppice gate
When Frost was spectre-gray,
And Winter’s dregs made desolate
The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky
Like strings from broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
Had sought their household fires.

The land’s sharp features seemed to be
The Century’s corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
Seemed fervourless as I.

At once a voice outburst among
The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
Of joy illimited;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
Upon the growing gloom.

So little cause for carollings
Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
And I was unaware.
```

text_map.central_idea: On a desolate winter evening that feels like the funeral of the dying century, a speaker who feels as lifeless as the land hears a frail old thrush pour out a joyful song.
```passage
    North Richmond Street, being blind, was a quiet
street except at the hour when the Christian Brothers’
School set the boys free. An uninhabited house of two
storeys stood at the blind end, detached from its
neighbours in a square ground. The other houses of the
street, conscious of decent lives within them, gazed at
one another with brown imperturbable faces.

    The former tenant of our house, a priest, had died
in the back drawing-room. Air, musty from having been
long enclosed, hung in all the rooms, and the waste room
behind the kitchen was littered with old useless papers.
Among these I found a few paper-covered books, the pages
of which were curled and damp: The Abbot, by Walter
Scott, The Devout Communicant and The Memoirs of Vidocq.
I liked the last best because its leaves were yellow.
The wild garden behind the house contained a central
apple-tree and a few straggling bushes under one of
which I found the late tenant’s rusty bicycle-pump. He
had been a very charitable priest; in his will he had
left all his money to institutions and the furniture of
his house to his sister.

    When the short days of winter came dusk fell before
we had well eaten our dinners. When we met in the street
the houses had grown sombre. The space of sky above us
was the colour of ever-changing violet and towards it
the lamps of the street lifted their feeble lanterns.
The cold air stung us and we played till our bodies
glowed. Our shouts echoed in the silent street. The
career of our play brought us through the dark muddy
lanes behind the houses where we ran the gauntlet of the
rough tribes from the cottages, to the back doors of the
dark dripping gardens where odours arose from the
ashpits, to the dark odorous stables where a coachman
smoothed and combed the horse or shook music from the
buckled harness. When we returned to the street light
from the kitchen windows had filled the areas. If my
uncle was seen turning the corner we hid in the shadow
until we had seen him safely housed. Or if Mangan’s
sister came out on the doorstep to call her brother in
to his tea we watched her from our shadow peer up and
down the street. We waited to see whether she would
remain or go in and, if she remained, we left our shadow
and walked up to Mangan’s steps resignedly. She was
waiting for us, her figure defined by the light from the
half-opened door. Her brother always teased her before
he obeyed and I stood by the railings looking at her.
Her dress swung as she moved her body and the soft rope
of her hair tossed from side to side.

    Every morning I lay on the floor in the front
parlour watching her door. The blind was pulled down to
within an inch of the sash so that I could not be seen.
When she came out on the doorstep my heart leaped. I ran
to the hall, seized my books and followed her. I kept
her brown figure always in my eye and, when we came near
the point at which our ways diverged, I quickened my
pace and passed her. This happened morning after
morning. I had never spoken to her, except for a few
casual words, and yet her name was like a summons to all
my foolish blood.

    Her image accompanied me even in places the most
hostile to romance. On Saturday evenings when my aunt
went marketing I had to go to carry some of the parcels.
We walked through the flaring streets, jostled by
drunken men and bargaining women, amid the curses of
labourers, the shrill litanies of shop-boys who stood on
guard by the barrels of pigs’ cheeks, the nasal chanting
of street-singers, who sang a come-all-you about
O’Donovan Rossa, or a ballad about the troubles in our
native land. These noises converged in a single
sensation of life for me: I imagined that I bore my
chalice safely through a throng of foes. Her name sprang
to my lips at moments in strange prayers and praises
which I myself did not understand. My eyes were often
full of tears (I could not tell why) and at times a
flood from my heart seemed to pour itself out into my
bosom. I thought little of the future. I did not know
whether I would ever speak to her or not or, if I spoke
to her, how I could tell her of my confused adoration.
But my body was like a harp and her words and gestures
were like fingers running upon the wires.
```

The following passage from a short story is by Katherine Mansfield (1920). This is an excerpt.

```passage
    Although it was so brilliantly fine—the blue sky
powdered with gold and great spots of light like white
wine splashed over the Jardins Publiques—Miss Brill was
glad that she had decided on her fur. The air was
motionless, but when you opened your mouth there was
just a faint chill, like a chill from a glass of iced
water before you sip, and now and again a leaf came
drifting—from nowhere, from the sky. Miss Brill put up
her hand and touched her fur. Dear little thing! It was
nice to feel it again. She had taken it out of its box
that afternoon, shaken out the moth-powder, given it a
good brush, and rubbed the life back into the dim little
eyes. “What has been happening to me?” said the sad
little eyes. Oh, how sweet it was to see them snap at
her again from the red eiderdown!... But the nose, which
was of some black composition, wasn’t at all firm. It
must have had a knock, somehow. Never mind—a little dab
of black sealing-wax when the time came—when it was
absolutely necessary.... Little rogue! Yes, she really
felt like that about it. Little rogue biting its tail
just by her left ear. She could have taken it off and
laid it on her lap and stroked it. She felt a tingling
in her hands and arms, but that came from walking, she
supposed. And when she breathed, something light and
sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle seemed to move
in her bosom.

    There were a number of people out this afternoon,
far more than last Sunday. And the band sounded louder
and gayer. That was because the Season had begun. For
although the band played all the year round on Sundays,
out of season it was never the same. It was like some
one playing with only the family to listen; it didn’t
care how it played if there weren’t any strangers
present. Wasn’t the conductor wearing a new coat, too?
She was sure it was new. He scraped with his foot and
flapped his arms like a rooster about to crow, and the
bandsmen sitting in the green rotunda blew out their
cheeks and glared at the music. Now there came a little
“flutey” bit—very pretty!—a little chain of bright
drops. She was sure it would be repeated. It was; she
lifted her head and smiled.

    Only two people shared her “special” seat: a fine
old man in a velvet coat, his hands clasped over a huge
carved walking-stick, and a big old woman, sitting
upright, with a roll of knitting on her embroidered
apron. They did not speak. This was disappointing, for
Miss Brill always looked forward to the conversation.
She had become really quite expert, she thought, at
listening as though she didn’t listen, at sitting in
other people’s lives just for a minute while they talked
round her.

    She glanced, sideways, at the old couple. Perhaps
they would go soon. Last Sunday, too, hadn’t been as
interesting as usual. An Englishman and his wife, he
wearing a dreadful Panama hat and she button boots. And
she’d gone on the whole time about how she ought to wear
spectacles; she knew she needed them; but that it was no
good getting any; they’d be sure to break and they’d
never keep on. And he’d been so patient. He’d suggested
everything—gold rims, the kind that curved round your
ears, little pads inside the bridge. No, nothing would
please her. “They’ll always be sliding down my nose!”
Miss Brill had wanted to shake her.

    The old people sat on the bench, still as statues.
Never mind, there was always the crowd to watch. To and
fro, in front of the flower-beds and the band rotunda,
the couples and groups paraded, stopped to talk, to
greet, to buy a handful of flowers from the old beggar
who had his tray fixed to the railings. Little children
ran among them, swooping and laughing; little boys with
big white silk bows under their chins, little girls,
little French dolls, dressed up in velvet and lace. And
sometimes a tiny staggerer came suddenly rocking into
the open from under the trees, stopped, stared, as
suddenly sat down “flop,” until its small high-stepping
mother, like a young hen, rushed scolding to its rescue.
Other people sat on the benches and green chairs, but
they were nearly always the same, Sunday after Sunday,
and—Miss Brill had often noticed—there was something
funny about nearly all of them. They were odd, silent,
nearly all old, and from the way they stared they looked
as though they’d just come from dark little rooms or
even—even cupboards!
```

ears, little pads inside the bridge. No, nothing would
please her. “They’ll always be sliding down my nose!”
Miss Brill had wanted to shake her.
The old people sat on the bench, still as statues.
Never mind, there was always the crowd to watch. To and
fro, in front of the flower-beds and the band rotunda,
the couples and groups paraded, stopped to talk, to
greet, to buy a handful of flowers from the old beggar
who had his tray fixed to the railings. Little children
ran among them, swooping and laughing; little boys with
big white silk bows under their chins, little girls,
little French dolls, dressed up in velvet and lace. And
sometimes a tiny staggerer came suddenly rocking into
the open from under the trees, stopped, stared, as
suddenly sat down “flop,” until its small high-stepping
mother, like a young hen, rushed scolding to its rescue.
Other people sat on the benches and green chairs, but
they were nearly always the same, Sunday after Sunday,
and—Miss Brill had often noticed—there was something
funny about nearly all of them. They were odd, silent,
nearly all old, and from the way they stared they looked
as though they’d just come from dark little rooms or
even—even cupboards!

text_map.central_idea: On a bright Sunday at the start of the Season, Miss Brill takes pleasure in her worn fur, the band and the crowd in the public gardens. She lives through other people's lives by watching them. Her lively, sympathetic narration contains signs she cannot read: her sadness, her shabbiness and her own place among the odd, silent, aging bench-sitters she finds 'funny.'
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A third-person limited narrator who stays very close to Miss Brill and often slips into her own phrasing (free indirect discourse). The reader shares her delighted view and can also see ironies about her that she misses.

```passage
    ALGERNON. Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?

    LANE. I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.

    ALGERNON. I’m sorry for that, for your sake. I don’t
play accurately—any one can play accurately—but I play
with wonderful expression. As far as the piano is
concerned, sentiment is my forte. I keep science for
Life.

    LANE. Yes, sir.

    ALGERNON. And, speaking of the science of Life, have
you got the cucumber sandwiches cut for Lady Bracknell?

    LANE. Yes, sir. [Hands them on a salver.]

    ALGERNON. [Inspects them, takes two, and sits down
on the sofa.] Oh! . . . by the way, Lane, I see from
your book that on Thursday night, when Lord Shoreman and
Mr. Worthing were dining with me, eight bottles of
champagne are entered as having been consumed.

    LANE. Yes, sir; eight bottles and a pint.

    ALGERNON. Why is it that at a bachelor’s
establishment the servants invariably drink the
champagne? I ask merely for information.

    LANE. I attribute it to the superior quality of the
wine, sir. I have often observed that in married
households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate
brand.

    ALGERNON. Good heavens! Is marriage so demoralising
as that?

    LANE. I believe it is a very pleasant state, sir. I
have had very little experience of it myself up to the
present. I have only been married once. That was in
consequence of a misunderstanding between myself and a
young person.

    ALGERNON. [Languidly.] I don’t know that I am much
interested in your family life, Lane.

    LANE. No, sir; it is not a very interesting subject.
I never think of it myself.

    ALGERNON. Very natural, I am sure. That will do,
Lane, thank you.

    LANE. Thank you, sir. [Lane goes out.]

    ALGERNON. Lane’s views on marriage seem somewhat
lax. Really, if the lower orders don’t set us a good
example, what on earth is the use of them? They seem, as
a class, to have absolutely no sense of moral
responsibility.

    [Enter Lane.]

    LANE. Mr. Ernest Worthing.

    [Enter Jack.]

    [Lane goes out.]

    ALGERNON. How are you, my dear Ernest? What brings
you up to town?

    JACK. Oh, pleasure, pleasure! What else should bring
one anywhere? Eating as usual, I see, Algy!

    ALGERNON. [Stiffly.] I believe it is customary in
good society to take some slight refreshment at five
o’clock. Where have you been since last Thursday?

    JACK. [Sitting down on the sofa.] In the country.

    ALGERNON. What on earth do you do there?

    JACK. [Pulling off his gloves.] When one is in town
one amuses oneself. When one is in the country one
amuses other people. It is excessively boring.

    ALGERNON. And who are the people you amuse?

    JACK. [Airily.] Oh, neighbours, neighbours.

    ALGERNON. Got nice neighbours in your part of
Shropshire?

    JACK. Perfectly horrid! Never speak to one of them.

    ALGERNON. How immensely you must amuse them! [Goes
over and takes sandwich.] By the way, Shropshire is your
county, is it not?

    JACK. Eh? Shropshire? Yes, of course. Hallo! Why all
these cups? Why cucumber sandwiches? Why such reckless
extravagance in one so young? Who is coming to tea?

    ALGERNON. Oh! merely Aunt Augusta and Gwendolen.

    JACK. How perfectly delightful!

    ALGERNON. Yes, that is all very well; but I am
afraid Aunt Augusta won’t quite approve of your being
here.

    JACK. May I ask why?

    ALGERNON. My dear fellow, the way you flirt with
Gwendolen is perfectly disgraceful. It is almost as bad
as the way Gwendolen flirts with you.

    JACK. I am in love with Gwendolen. I have come up to
town expressly to propose to her.

    ALGERNON. I thought you had come up for pleasure? .
. . I call that business.

    JACK. How utterly unromantic you are!

    ALGERNON. I really don’t see anything romantic in
proposing. It is very romantic to be in love. But there
is nothing romantic about a definite proposal. Why, one
may be accepted. One usually is, I believe. Then the
excitement is all over. The very essence of romance is
uncertainty. If ever I get married, I’ll certainly try
to forget the fact.

    JACK. I have no doubt about that, dear Algy. The
Divorce Court was specially invented for people whose
memories are so curiously constituted.

    ALGERNON. Oh! there is no use speculating on that
subject. Divorces are made in Heaven—[Jack puts out his
hand to take a sandwich. Algernon at once interferes.]
Please don’t touch the cucumber sandwiches. They are
ordered specially for Aunt Augusta. [Takes one and eats
it.]

    JACK. Well, you have been eating them all the time.

    ALGERNON. That is quite a different matter. She is
my aunt. [Takes plate from below.] Have some bread and
butter. The bread and butter is for Gwendolen. Gwendolen
is devoted to bread and butter.

    JACK. [Advancing to table and helping himself.] And
very good bread and butter it is too.

    ALGERNON. Well, my dear fellow, you need not eat as
if you were going to eat it all. You behave as if you
were married to her already. You are not married to her
already, and I don’t think you ever will be.
```

text_map.central_idea: Through epigrams that turn conventional values upside down, the opening conversation mocks the upper-class idea of marriage, morality and good manners. Algernon preaches rules that he excuses himself from, Lane deflects his master with deadpan wit, and Jack's answers about his name and his county hint that he is hiding something.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: There is no narrator. This is dramatic dialogue between Algernon, his manservant Lane and his friend Jack, with stage directions that sometimes give information the dialogue does not, such as labeling the man announced as Ernest with the name JACK.

payload.set_intro:
Public-domain source text — Robert Frost, An Old Man's Winter Night, Mountain Interval (New York: Henry Holt, 1916)
An Old Man's Winter Night
by Robert Frost
The following poem is by Robert Frost (1916).

```passage
All out of doors looked darkly in at him
Through the thin frost, almost in separate stars,
That gathers on the pane in empty rooms.
What kept his eyes from giving back the gaze
Was the lamp tilted near them in his hand.
What kept him from remembering what it was
That brought him to that creaking room was age.
He stood with barrels round him--at a loss.
And having scared the cellar under him
In clomping there, he scared it once again
In clomping off;--and scared the outer night,
Which has its sounds, familiar, like the roar
Of trees and crack of branches, common things,
But nothing so like beating on a box.
A light he was to no one but himself
Where now he sat, concerned with he knew what,
A quiet light, and then not even that.
He consigned to the moon, such as she was,
So late-arising, to the broken moon
As better than the sun in any case
For such a charge, his snow upon the roof,
His icicles along the wall to keep;
And slept. The log that shifted with a jolt
Once in the stove, disturbed him and he shifted,
And eased his heavy breathing, but still slept.
One aged man--one man--can't fill a house,
A farm, a countryside, or if he can,
It's thus he does it of a winter night.
```

parts.prompt:
The following poem is "An Old Man's Winter Night" by Robert Frost (1916). In this poem, the speaker describes an elderly man alone in his farmhouse on a winter night, following him from his confused visit to the cellar to his falling asleep by the stove while the dark, cold world presses in around the house.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Robert Frost uses poetic elements and techniques to convey a complex view of the old man's solitude, in which his frailty, forgetfulness, and smallness against the vast winter night exist alongside a quiet, almost stubborn claim that his lone presence still keeps and fills the place.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Frost's old man is easy to pity. He forgets why he went to the cellar, he cannot meet the stare of the night, and by the end even his lamp is gone. But the poem does not let pity have the last word. Through personification, tangled syntax, and shrinking repetition, Frost shows a man reduced almost to nothing. Yet through possessive language and a final hedged statement, he insists that this reduced man still holds his house against the dark, and that holding it this way, half-asleep and barely visible, may be the only way anyone could.

The opening makes the man an object instead of an observer. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" turns the whole winter world into a watcher, and the lamp "tilted near" his eyes keeps him from "giving back the gaze." The light that should help him see actually blinds him to what is outside, so from the first lines his one defense against the dark is also what isolates him. Frost then lets the sentence structure act out his confusion. "What kept him from remembering what it was" circles through two "what" clauses before it finally lands on "age," so the reader, like the man, has to grope for the point. When the line arrives at "at a loss," the dash before it works like a stall in his thinking, a blank where his purpose should be.

What makes this more than a portrait of decline is the speaker's dry humor. The man "scared the cellar under him / In clomping there," then scared it "once again" on the way out. "Clomping" is a clumsy, almost cartoonish word, and frightening a cellar is funny. But the joke turns when he scares "the outer night" too. The night knows the "roar / Of trees and crack of branches, common things," yet has heard nothing "so like beating on a box." The simile deflates him and is oddly proud of him at once: his noise is a hollow knocking, but it is also unlike anything in nature. For a moment the vast night is the one startled. Frost lets us laugh at the man without mocking him, because the small noise really does register.

The middle of the poem shrinks him through repetition. "A light he was to no one but himself" already narrows his reach, and "A quiet light, and then not even that" erases it. The word "light" dims every time it comes back. Read alone, this sounds like death, and the poem seems to lean that way. But Frost pulls back: the man "slept," shifts when a log jolts in the stove, and "still slept." "Still" means both motionless and continuing, so the poem gestures toward death while keeping him alive.

Even asleep, he claims ownership. He hands "his snow upon the roof, / His icicles along the wall" to the moon to keep. The possessives are stubborn, since snow and ice belong to no one, yet he treats them as property under his watch. His chosen keeper is "the broken moon," late and partial, "As better than the sun." A broken guardian fits a broken man, and his choice suggests he understands that diminished things can still do a job.

The last three lines rescale everything. "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house" sounds like a verdict, the repetition stripping him down to a single "one." Then the list widens to "A farm, a countryside," and the hedge "or if he can" reopens the question. "It's thus he does it of a winter night" points back to everything we have watched: the forgetting, the clomping, the fading light, the sleep. That is the filling. It is hollow, like the box, but it is real, because no one else is there to do it. The poem ends in neither pity nor celebration but in a grudging respect for presence at its smallest.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the poem presents the old man's solitude, and it must go beyond saying the poem is 'about loneliness' or 'about old age.' Strong theses identify a tension, for example that the man is pitiably reduced (forgetful, dimming, outmatched by the night) yet also asserts a stubborn, limited power to keep house against the dark, or that the final lines turn pity into qualified respect. A thesis that only lists devices ('Frost uses imagery and personification'), only restates the prompt, or makes a claim the text cannot support (for example that the man definitely dies in the poem, or that the poem is simply celebratory) does not earn the point. The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere, but it must be identifiable.

Strong responses (3-4 points) select specific evidence from across the poem and explain how it builds the divided view: the personified night that 'looked darkly in at him' and the gaze he cannot return; the convoluted syntax of 'What kept him from remembering what it was' that enacts his confusion; the caesura in 'at a loss'; the comic-pathetic 'clomping' and the simile 'like beating on a box' that make his noise both intrusive and absurd against the night's 'common things'; the shrinking repetition of 'A light he was to no one but himself' and 'A quiet light, and then not even that'; the possessives 'his snow' and 'His icicles' entrusted to the 'broken moon'; and the concluding qualified claim 'can't fill a house... or if he can.' Commentary must connect each choice to the line of reasoning (how it shows diminishment, how it shows persistence or ownership, or how the two interact) rather than labeling devices or paraphrasing. A 2 typically offers accurate but general commentary or focuses only on loneliness and decay; a 1 mostly summarizes the old man's actions; a 0 is off-topic or mere restatement. Responses that track the movement of the poem, from the man as observed object to the final assertion, generally reason more effectively than device-by-device lists.

Sophistication may be earned by exploring the poem's complexity, for example by showing how the last three lines rescale the poem (house, farm, countryside) and recast everything before them, so that 'thus he does it' names both a hollow, fragile filling and a real one; by analyzing how the speaker's tone balances pity with dry humor (the scared cellar, the box) without mocking him; by examining the ambiguity of the light going out and the man sleeping 'still,' noting how the poem gestures toward death without stating it; or by considering how the 'broken moon' as a fitting keeper mirrors the man's own brokenness. Writing that is especially vivid and controlled in service of such an argument can also qualify. A single sweeping statement or an unsupported claim about Frost's life or rural America does not earn the point.

In "An Old Man's Winter Night," Robert Frost presents an old man who is weak, forgetful, and small compared to the huge cold night outside, but who still manages, in a small way, to hold onto his house. The poem pities him, yet by the end it also gives him a kind of quiet dignity, and Frost shows both through imagery, sound, and the way the poem ends.

At the start the man is shown as someone being watched instead of someone acting. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" makes the night into a person who stares at the house, and the old man cannot stare back because "the lamp tilted near them in his hand" blocks his eyes. This makes him seem weak, since he is outmatched by the dark and does not even see how big it is. His forgetfulness is also shown by the sentence "What kept him from remembering what it was." The sentence is long and twisting, so the reader gets a little lost like he does, and the line "He stood with barrels round him--at a loss" stops with a dash to show him stuck in the cellar. The barrels surround him and make him look small.

Frost also uses sound to make him seem both silly and sad. The word "clomping" is heavy and clumsy, and the poem says he "scared the cellar under him." This is almost funny, since the cellar is scared of an old man, but it also shows how his noise is out of place. The night has "common things" like the roar of trees, and compared to that his noise is "like beating on a box." The simile makes him sound hollow and small, like he is only banging on something empty.

The poem then gets quieter. "A light he was to no one but himself" and then "A quiet light, and then not even that" shrink him step by step until the light seems to go out, which could hint at death, though he is really just asleep. Still, the man does not disappear. He gives his "snow" and "icicles" to the moon to keep, and the words "his" and "His" show he thinks of them as belonging to him. The "broken moon" is a fitting guard because it is damaged like he is.

The repetition of "one man" stresses how little he is, but the "or if he can" lets in a doubt. lit_frq.title: Poetry Analysis: An Old Man's Winter Night

prompt.lead: The following poem is "An Old Man's Winter Night" by Robert Frost (1916). In this poem, the speaker describes an elderly man alone in his farmhouse on a winter night, following him from his confused visit to the cellar to his falling asleep by the stove while the dark, cold world presses in around the house.
prompt.task: Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Robert Frost uses poetic elements and techniques to convey a complex view of the old man's solitude, in which his frailty, forgetfulness, and smallness against the vast winter night exist alongside a quiet, almost stubborn claim that his lone presence still keeps and fills the place.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: An Old Man's Winter Night
passage.headnote: The following poem is by Robert Frost (1916).
stanzas: All out of doors looked darkly in at him
Through the thin frost, almost in separate stars,
That gathers on the pane in empty rooms.
What kept his eyes from giving back the gaze
Was the lamp tilted near them in his hand.
What kept him from remembering what it was
That brought him to that creaking room was age.
He stood with barrels round him--at a loss.
And having scared the cellar under him
In clomping there, he scared it once again
In clomping off;--and scared the outer night,
Which has its sounds, familiar, like the roar
Of trees and crack of branches, common things,
But nothing so like beating on a box.
A light he was to no one but himself
Where now he sat, concerned with he knew what,
A quiet light, and then not even that.
He consigned to the moon, such as she was,
So late-arising, to the broken moon
As better than the sun in any case
For such a charge, his snow upon the roof,
His icicles along the wall to keep;
And slept. The log that shifted with a jolt
Once in the stove, disturbed him and he shifted,
And eased his heavy breathing, but still slept.
One aged man--one man--can't fill a house,
A farm, a countryside, or if he can,
It's thus he does it of a winter night.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the poem presents the old man's solitude, and it must go beyond saying the poem is 'about loneliness' or 'about old age.' Strong theses identify a tension, for example that the man is pitiably reduced (forgetful, dimming, outmatched by the night) yet also asserts a stubborn, limited power to keep house against the dark, or that the final lines turn pity into qualified respect. A thesis that only lists devices ('Frost uses imagery and personification'), only restates the prompt, or makes a claim the text cannot support (for example that the man definitely dies in the poem, or that the poem is simply celebratory) does not earn the point. The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere, but it must be identifiable.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses (3-4 points) select specific evidence from across the poem and explain how it builds the divided view: the personified night that 'looked darkly in at him' and the gaze he cannot return; the convoluted syntax of 'What kept him from remembering what it was' that enacts his confusion; the caesura in 'at a loss'; the comic-pathetic 'clomping' and the simile 'like beating on a box' that make his noise both intrusive and absurd against the night's 'common things'; the shrinking repetition of 'A light he was to no one but himself' and 'A quiet light, and then not even that'; the possessives 'his snow' and 'His icicles' entrusted to the 'broken moon'; and the concluding qualified claim 'can't fill a house... or if he can.' Commentary must connect each choice to the line of reasoning (how it shows diminishment, how it shows persistence or ownership, or how the two interact) rather than labeling devices or paraphrasing. A 2 typically offers accurate but general commentary or focuses only on loneliness and decay; a 1 mostly summarizes the old man's actions; a 0 is off-topic or mere restatement. Responses that track the movement of the poem, from the man as observed object to the final assertion, generally reason more effectively than device-by-device lists.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication may be earned by exploring the poem's complexity, for example by showing how the last three lines rescale the poem (house, farm, countryside) and recast everything before them, so that 'thus he does it' names both a hollow, fragile filling and a real one; by analyzing how the speaker's tone balances pity with dry humor (the scared cellar, the box) without mocking him; by examining the ambiguity of the light going out and the man sleeping 'still,' noting how the poem gestures toward death without stating it; or by considering how the 'broken moon' as a fitting keeper mirrors the man's own brokenness. Writing that is especially vivid and controlled in service of such an argument can also qualify. A single sweeping statement or an unsupported claim about Frost's life or rural America does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Do not reward claims that the old man dies as settled fact; the text says he 'still slept.' Discussing the poem's hints of death as an ambiguity is acceptable and can be strong.
Biographical claims about Frost or historical claims not grounded in the text should not earn credit as evidence.
Responses need not address every line; depth of commentary on well-chosen evidence outweighs coverage.
Identifying devices with correct terminology is not required; what matters is explaining how specific choices create meaning related to the focus.

A response that reads the poem as purely bleak can still earn Row A and solid Row B credit if well argued, but responses that grapple with the final lines' qualified assertion are better placed for higher B scores and C.

defensible_positions: The poem mainly presents the old man as diminished and isolated: the night watches him, his memory fails, his light shrinks to nothing, and the final lines grant him only a hollow, ironic power to 'fill' the house.

The poem moves from pity toward qualified respect: though frail and forgetful, the man claims ownership ('his snow,' 'His icicles') and, through his mere presence and noise, holds the house against the night in the only way one person can.
The speaker balances pathos with gentle humor, so that the man's clomping and box-like noise seem both absurd and touching, keeping the poem from either sentimentality or mockery.
The poem uses sleep and the fading light to gesture toward death, so that the man's keeping of the house is shown as precarious and temporary even as it is affirmed.
The poem contrasts the vast, indifferent natural world (night, trees, broken moon) with the small human presence, suggesting that human meaning is limited and fragile but still real.

devices.quote: All out of doors looked darkly in at him
devices.effect: Makes the night a watching presence pressing in on the house, casting the man as observed and exposed, and setting up the contest between his small presence and the vast outside.

devices.quote: Through the thin frost, almost in separate stars,
devices.effect: The frost on the window looks like a cold, distant sky, fusing the windowpane with the cosmos and stressing how thin the barrier is between the man and the emptiness outside.

devices.quote: That brought him to that creaking room was age.
devices.effect: The long, winding sentence holds back its subject until the last word, 'age,' acting out the man's lapse of memory and landing on the cause flatly.

devices.quote: He stood with barrels round him--at a loss.
devices.effect: The dash forces a pause that copies his stalled confusion, leaving him stranded among the objects of the cellar.

devices.quote: he scared it once again
devices.effect: The repeated 'scared' and 'clomping' give his movement a clumsy, slightly comic insistence, so his noise is the way he asserts himself, however awkwardly.

devices.quote: But nothing so like beating on a box.
devices.effect: Sets the man's hollow, unnatural sound apart from the night's 'common things,' making him both intrusive and pitiably small, a noise the natural world does not recognize.

devices.quote: A quiet light, and then not even that.
devices.effect: Picking up 'A light he was to no one but himself,' the repeated and shrinking light traces his fading presence, literally the lamp going out and figuratively a hint of mortality.

devices.quote: to the broken moon
devices.effect: Entrusting his house to a damaged, 'late-arising' moon pictures a guardian as worn as he is, a fitting but uncertain stand-in for his watchfulness.

devices.quote: His icicles along the wall to keep;
devices.effect: The possessive 'His' (echoing 'his snow') claims ownership even over winter's cold, suggesting dignity and stubborn stewardship in the middle of decline.

devices.quote: One aged man--one man--can't fill a house,
devices.effect: The halting self-correction and plain denial make the closing claim modest, and so the qualified turn that follows feels earned rather than sentimental.

devices.quote: It's thus he does it of a winter night.
devices.effect: The closing line turns the poem's pity into a wry, qualified affirmation, recasting all his fumbling, noise, and sleep as the way a single life fills a place.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing the old man's actions in order without explaining how the language shapes our view of him.
Stating as fact that the old man dies, ignoring 'but still slept,' instead of treating the death imagery as suggestion or ambiguity.
Reading the poem as only sad or only uplifting, and so missing the tension the final lines create.
Listing devices (personification, imagery, repetition) without tying them to a claim about solitude, diminishment, or presence.
Bringing in unsupported biographical claims about Frost or general claims about rural life in place of textual evidence.
Ignoring the final three lines, which change the meaning of the whole poem.

samples.essay:
Frost's old man is easy to pity. He forgets why he went to the cellar, he cannot meet the stare of the night, and by the end even his lamp is gone. But the poem does not let pity have the last word. Through personification, tangled syntax, and shrinking repetition, Frost shows a man reduced almost to nothing. Yet through possessive language and a final hedged statement, he insists that this reduced man still holds his house against the dark, and that holding it this way, half-asleep and barely visible, may be the only way anyone could.

The opening makes the man an object instead of an observer. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" turns the whole winter world into a watcher, and the lamp "tilted near" his eyes keeps him from "giving back the gaze." The light that should help him see actually blinds him to what is outside, so from the first lines his one defense against the dark is also what isolates him. Frost then lets the sentence structure act out his confusion. "What kept him from remembering what it was" circles through two "what" clauses before it finally lands on "age," so the reader, like the man, has to grope for the point. When the line arrives at "at a loss," the dash before it works like a stall in his thinking, a blank where his purpose should be.

What makes this more than a portrait of decline is the speaker's dry humor. The man "scared the cellar under him / In clomping there," then scared it "once again" on the way out. "Clomping" is a clumsy, almost cartoonish word, and frightening a cellar is funny. But the joke turns when he scares "the outer night" too. The night knows the "roar / Of trees and crack of branches, common things," yet has heard nothing "so like beating on a box." The simile deflates him and is oddly proud of him at once: his noise is a hollow knocking, but it is also unlike anything in nature. For a moment the vast night is the one startled. Frost lets us laugh at the man without mocking him, because the small noise really does register.

The middle of the poem shrinks him through repetition. "A light he was to no one but himself" already narrows his reach, and "A quiet light, and then not even that" erases it. The word "light" dims every time it comes back. Read alone, this sounds like death, and the poem seems to lean that way. But Frost pulls back: the man "slept," shifts when a log jolts in the stove, and "still slept." "Still" means both motionless and continuing, so the poem gestures toward death while keeping him alive.

Even asleep, he claims ownership. He hands "his snow upon the roof, / His icicles along the wall" to the moon to keep. The possessives are stubborn, since snow and ice belong to no one, yet he treats them as property under his watch. His chosen keeper is "the broken moon," late and partial, "As better than the sun." A broken guardian fits a broken man, and his choice suggests he understands that diminished things can still do a job.

The last three lines rescale everything. "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house" sounds like a verdict, the repetition stripping him down to a single "one." Then the list widens to "A farm, a countryside," and the hedge "or if he can" reopens the question. "It's thus he does it of a winter night" points back to everything we have watched: the forgetting, the clomping, the fading light, the sleep. That is the filling. It is hollow, like the box, but it is real, because no one else is there to do it. The poem ends in neither pity nor celebration but in a grudging respect for presence at its smallest.

In "An Old Man's Winter Night," Robert Frost presents an old man who is weak, forgetful, and small compared to the huge cold night outside, but who still manages, in a small way, to hold onto his house. The poem pities him, yet by the end it also gives him a kind of quiet dignity, and Frost shows both through imagery, sound, and the way the poem ends.

At the start the man is shown as someone being watched instead of someone acting. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" makes the night into a person who stares at the house, and the old man cannot stare back because "the lamp tilted near them in his hand" blocks his eyes. This makes him seem weak, since he is outmatched by the dark and does not even see how big it is. His forgetfulness is also shown by the sentence "What kept him from remembering what it was." The sentence is long and twisting, so the reader gets a little lost like he does, and the line "He stood with barrels round him--at a loss" stops with a dash to show him stuck in the cellar. The barrels surround him and make him look small.

Frost also uses sound to make him seem both silly and sad. The word "clomping" is heavy and clumsy, and the poem says he "scared the cellar under him." This is almost funny, since the cellar is scared of an old man, but it also shows how his noise is out of place. The night has "common things" like the roar of trees, and compared to that his noise is "like beating on a box." The simile makes him sound hollow and small, like he is only banging on something empty.

The poem then gets quieter. "A light he was to no one but himself" and then "A quiet light, and then not even that" shrink him step by step until the light seems to go out, which could hint at death, though he is really just asleep. Still, the man does not disappear. He gives his "snow" and "icicles" to the moon to keep, and the words "his" and "His" show he thinks of them as belonging to him. The "broken moon" is a fitting guard because it is damaged like he is.

The last lines say "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house," but then add "or if he can, / It's thus he does it of a winter night." The repetition of "one man" stresses how little he is, but the "or if he can" lets in a doubt. In the end Frost suggests that the old man fills the place only barely, by being there, sleeping and breathing in the cold, and that this is small but still real.

```passage
    Mr. Ryder might aptly be called the dean of the Blue
Veins. The original Blue Veins were a little society of
colored persons organized in a certain Northern city
shortly after the war. Its purpose was to establish and
maintain correct social standards among a people whose
social condition presented almost unlimited room for
improvement. By accident, combined perhaps with some
natural affinity, the society consisted of individuals
who were, generally speaking, more white than black.
Some envious outsider made the suggestion that no one
was eligible for membership who was not white enough to
show blue veins. The suggestion was readily adopted by
those who were not of the favored few, and since that
time the society, though possessing a longer and more
pretentious name, had been known far and wide as the
"Blue Vein Society," and its members as the "Blue
Veins."

    The Blue Veins did not allow that any such
requirement existed for admission to their circle, but,
on the contrary, declared that character and culture
were the only things considered; and that if most of
their members were light-colored, it was because such
persons, as a rule, had had better opportunities to
qualify themselves for membership. Opinions differed,
too, as to the usefulness of the society. There were
those who had been known to assail it violently as a
glaring example of the very prejudice from which the
colored race had suffered most; and later, when such
critics had succeeded in getting on the inside, they had
been heard to maintain with zeal and earnestness that
the society was a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a
shield,--a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night,
to guide their people through the social wilderness.
Another alleged prerequisite for Blue Vein membership
was that of free birth; and while there was really no
such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of
the members would have been unable to meet it if there
had been. If there were one or two of the older members
who had come up from the South and from slavery, their
history presented enough romantic circumstances to rob
their servile origin of its grosser aspects.

    While there were no such tests of eligibility, it is
true that the Blue Veins had their notions on these
subjects, and that not all of them were equally liberal
in regard to the things they collectively disclaimed.
Mr. Ryder was one of the most conservative. Though he
had not been among the founders of the society, but had
come in some years later, his genius for social
leadership was such that he had speedily become its
recognized adviser and head, the custodian of its
standards, and the preserver of its traditions. He
shaped its social policy, was active in providing for
its entertainment, and when the interest fell off, as it
sometimes did, he fanned the embers until they burst
again into a cheerful flame.

    There were still other reasons for his popularity.
While he was not as white as some of the Blue Veins, his
appearance was such as to confer distinction upon them.
His features were of a refined type, his hair was almost
straight; he was always neatly dressed; his manners were
irreproachable, and his morals above suspicion. He had
come to Groveland a young man, and obtaining employment
in the office of a railroad company as messenger had in
time worked himself up to the position of stationery
clerk, having charge of the distribution of the office
supplies for the whole company. Although the lack of
early training had hindered the orderly development of a
naturally fine mind, it had not prevented him from doing
a great deal of reading or from forming decidedly
literary tastes. Poetry was his passion. He could repeat
whole pages of the great English poets; and if his
pronunciation was sometimes faulty, his eye, his voice,
his gestures, would respond to the changing sentiment
with a precision that revealed a poetic soul and
disarmed criticism. He was economical, and had saved
money; he owned and occupied a very comfortable house on
a respectable street. His residence was handsomely
furnished, containing among other things a good library,
especially rich in poetry, a piano, and some choice
engravings. He generally shared his house with some
young couple, who looked after his wants and were
company for him; for Mr. Ryder was a single man. In the
early days of his connection with the Blue Veins he had
been regarded as quite a catch, and young ladies and
their mothers had manoeuvred with much ingenuity to
capture him. Not, however, until Mrs. Molly Dixon
visited Groveland had any woman ever made him wish to
change his condition to that of a married man.
```

The following passage is from "The Wife of His Youth," a short story by Charles W. Chesnutt (1899 in the original). In this passage, the narrator describes the "Blue Vein Society," a social club of mostly light-skinned colored people founded in a Northern city shortly after the war, and introduces Mr. Ryder, its leading member.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Charles W. Chesnutt uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator's divided attitude toward the Blue Veins and Mr. Ryder, a measured respect for their ambition, refinement, and self-made success alongside quiet irony about the color and class prejudice they officially deny.

In the opening of "The Wife of His Youth," Chesnutt's narrator sounds a lot like a member of the club he is describing. He is courteous and measured, and he never quite accuses anyone of anything. That politeness is the joke. Through hedging syntax, denials that end up confirming what they deny, and a portrait of Mr. Ryder built out of concessions and inventories, the narrator gives the Blue Veins real credit for their ambition and refinement while letting their color prejudice show through the gaps in their own explanations. The irony stays quiet because it borrows the society's genteel manner, so the style ends up taking part in the respectability it questions.

The narrator's treatment of the society as a group depends on qualifiers. The members are light-skinned "By accident, combined perhaps with some natural affinity," a phrase that pretends to be neutral but slips. "By accident" and "perhaps" sound fair-minded, but "natural affinity" suggests that lightness is something the members are drawn to, a preference and not a coincidence. The nickname comes from "some envious outsider," which seems to dismiss it, yet it was "readily adopted," and a joke only spreads that fast if people think it is accurate. The society's official claim, that "character and culture were the only things considered," comes to us in indirect speech, so the narrator reports it without standing behind it. Still, he is not just mocking. The excuse that light-skinned people had "better opportunities" is partly true, given slavery's history, and the narrator lets it be both a plausible point and a convenient one.

The irony is sharpest with the critics who change sides once they get "on the inside." Their praise piles up into "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield," and the list is inflated past the point of meaning anything. Then the scriptural "pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night" turns a social club into the guide that led Israel out of Egypt. This exaggeration exposes how quickly principle gives way to belonging. But "the social wilderness" is not a totally empty phrase, because freed people after the war really were in an unfamiliar world. So the satire is aimed at the converts' zeal and not at the need the society answers. The same doubleness shows up in the sentence about free birth: "while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true" that few "would have been unable to meet it." The double negative and the long, winding clauses copy the society's own evasions. Even slavery gets edited, since "romantic circumstances" serve to "rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects." Painful history is rewritten as respectable romance, and the narrator's mild word "grosser" makes the cover-up sound like good taste.

Mr. Ryder gets a warmer but still ironic portrait. The language of office, "custodian of its standards, and the preserver of its traditions," honors his leadership, and the image of him fanning "the embers until they burst again into a cheerful flame" is honestly affectionate. Yet just before this the narrator calls him "one of the most conservative" about "the things they collectively disclaimed," so the standards he guards include the prejudice the group denies. The list of his traits makes this concrete: "his hair was almost straight" sits in the same series as "his morals above suspicion," and the parallel syntax treats nearness to whiteness as if it were a virtue. The word "almost" measures him on the same scale the society pretends it doesn't use. His rise from messenger to stationery clerk is real self-made success, though the grand phrasing about supplies "for the whole company" gently deflates it. The concession "if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty" leads into a soul that "disarmed criticism," and the narrator seems disarmed too. This shows the narrator smiling at how people change their opinion when they benefit.

passage.headnote: The following passage from a short story is by Charles W. Chesnutt (1899). This is an excerpt.
stanzas: Mr. Ryder might aptly be called the dean of the Blue
Veins. The original Blue Veins were a little society of
colored persons organized in a certain Northern city
shortly after the war. Its purpose was to establish and
maintain correct social standards among a people whose
social condition presented almost unlimited room for
improvement. By accident, combined perhaps with some
natural affinity, the society consisted of individuals
who were, generally speaking, more white than black.
Some envious outsider made the suggestion that no one
was eligible for membership who was not white enough to
show blue veins. The suggestion was readily adopted by
those who were not of the favored few, and since that
time the society, though possessing a longer and more
pretentious name, had been known far and wide as the
"Blue Vein Society," and its members as the "Blue
Veins."
The Blue Veins did not allow that any such
requirement existed for admission to their circle, but,
on the contrary, declared that character and culture
were the only things considered; and that if most of
their members were light-colored, it was because such
persons, as a rule, had had better opportunities to
qualify themselves for membership. Opinions differed,
too, as to the usefulness of the society. There were
those who had been known to assail it violently as a
glaring example of the very prejudice from which the
colored race had suffered most; and later, when such
critics had succeeded in getting on the inside, they had
been heard to maintain with zeal and earnestness that
the society was a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a
shield,--a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night,
to guide their people through the social wilderness.
Another alleged prerequisite for Blue Vein membership
was that of free birth; and while there was really no
such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of
the members would have been unable to meet it if there
had been. If there were one or two of the older members
who had come up from the South and from slavery, their
history presented enough romantic circumstances to rob
their servile origin of its grosser aspects.
While there were no such tests of eligibility, it is
true that the Blue Veins had their notions on these
subjects, and that not all of them were equally liberal
in regard to the things they collectively disclaimed.
Mr. Ryder was one of the most conservative. Though he
had not been among the founders of the society, but had
come in some years later, his genius for social
leadership was such that he had speedily become its
recognized adviser and head, the custodian of its
standards, and the preserver of its traditions. He
shaped its social policy, was active in providing for
its entertainment, and when the interest fell off, as it
sometimes did, he fanned the embers until they burst
again into a cheerful flame.
There were still other reasons for his popularity.
While he was not as white as some of the Blue Veins, his
appearance was such as to confer distinction upon them.
His features were of a refined type, his hair was almost
straight; he was always neatly dressed; his manners were
irreproachable, and his morals above suspicion. He had
come to Groveland a young man, and obtaining employment
in the office of a railroad company as messenger had in
time worked himself up to the position of stationery
clerk, having charge of the distribution of the office
supplies for the whole company. Although the lack of
early training had hindered the orderly development of a
naturally fine mind, it had not prevented him from doing
a great deal of reading or from forming decidedly
literary tastes. Poetry was his passion. He could repeat
whole pages of the great English poets; and if his
pronunciation was sometimes faulty, his eye, his voice,
his gestures, would respond to the changing sentiment
with a precision that revealed a poetic soul and
disarmed criticism. He was economical, and had saved
money; he owned and occupied a very comfortable house on
a respectable street. His residence was handsomely
furnished, containing among other things a good library,
especially rich in poetry, a piano, and some choice
engravings. He generally shared his house with some
young couple, who looked after his wants and were
company for him; for Mr. Ryder was a single man. In the
early days of his connection with the Blue Veins he had
been regarded as quite a catch, and young ladies and
their mothers had manoeuvred with much ingenuity to
capture him. Not, however, until Mrs. Molly Dixon
visited Groveland had any woman ever made him wish to
change his condition to that of a married man.

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication can be earned by working through the tension rather than settling it. Examples: arguing that the narrator's own genteel, Blue-Vein-like politeness is the tool of the satire, so the style takes part in what it mocks; explaining how Ryder can be both admirably self-made and complicit in the hierarchy he guards ('one of the most conservative'); seeing that the slavery passage ('rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects') shows the society reshaping painful history into respectable romance; or reading the final sentence about Mrs. Molly Dixon as a sign that personal desire will test Ryder's standards. The insight must run through the argument. A single complex-sounding sentence or speculation about the rest of the story without textual grounding does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Accept any reasonable wording for the narrator's attitude (ironic, wry, gently satirical, ambivalent, measured), as long as the response grounds it in specific language.
Do not reward claims about the author's biography or the rest of the story that are not supported by the passage and headnote.

Identifying the 'pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night' as a biblical allusion (the Exodus journey through the wilderness) is acceptable, but credit depends on explaining its inflated, ironic effect, not just labeling it.
Responses that read the narrator as straightforwardly endorsing the society's claim that 'character and culture were the only things considered' misread the irony and should be limited in Row B.
Discussion of race and colorism should stay tied to the text's own terms ('more white than black,' 'light-colored,' 'blue veins') and to the narrator's handling of them.

defensible_positions: The narrator's polite, judicious voice works as quiet satire: by repeating the society's denials in its own careful language, the narrator shows the color prejudice that the Blue Veins claim does not exist.

The narrator is divided: the passage takes seriously the Blue Veins' wish for 'correct social standards' and respects Ryder's self-made rise, but treats their ranking of people by lightness of skin and free birth as self-deception.

Mr. Ryder gets a warmer, more sympathetic portrait than the society as a whole, yet the irony still reaches him, since his 'distinction' rests partly on near-white features and his role is to guard exclusionary 'standards.'

The passage shows respectability as something staged and displayed (manners, possessions, recited poetry, rewritten histories of slavery), and the narrator both admires the effort and exposes what it costs and hides.
The ending turns from social portrait to personal desire with Mrs. Molly Dixon, suggesting that Ryder's carefully kept standards are about to be tested.

devices.quote: while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of the members would have been unable to meet it if there had been
devices.effect: The roundabout hedging denies the free-birth test while admitting that in practice it applies, so the society's claim exposes itself.

devices.quote: the society was a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield
devices.effect: The pile-up of grand rescue metaphors, spoken by former critics now 'on the inside,' mocks how self-interest changes opinion and inflates the society's importance.

devices.quote: a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night
devices.effect: The scriptural image of divine guidance through the wilderness is ironically oversized for a social club, which highlights the members' self-importance.

devices.quote: enough romantic circumstances to rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects
devices.effect: The genteel wording shows how members with slave origins are made acceptable by turning a painful history into a romance, which suggests shame about the past.

devices.quote: not all of them were equally liberal in regard to the things they collectively disclaimed
devices.effect: The mild phrasing shows the gap between the group's public denials and its members' private prejudices, and it prepares for Ryder's place among 'the most conservative.'

devices.quote: His features were of a refined type, his hair was almost straight; he was always neatly dressed; his manners were irreproachable, and his morals above suspicion.
devices.effect: The list puts racially coded physical traits on the same level as dress, manners, and morals, showing that the society treats closeness to whiteness as a virtue.

devices.quote: if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty, his eye, his voice, his gestures, would respond to the changing sentiment with a precision that revealed a poetic soul
devices.effect: Admitting a flaw and then giving real praise shows the narrator's sympathy for Ryder's self-education and gently notes the limits of his polish.

devices.quote: he fanned the embers until they burst again into a cheerful flame
devices.effect: Ryder's tireless social leadership appears as warm and life-giving, which supports a sincere side of the narrator's respect.

devices.quote: Not, however, until Mrs. Molly Dixon visited Groveland had any woman ever made him wish to change his condition to that of a married man.
devices.effect: The closing turn moves from portrait to plot and hints that desire will put Ryder's settled life and standards under pressure.

common_pitfalls: Taking the society's claim that 'character and culture were the only things considered' at face value and missing the narrator's irony.
Reading the narrator as harshly condemning, which ignores the real respect shown for Ryder's work, reading, and leadership.
Listing devices (irony, metaphor, allusion) without explaining how they shape the narrator's divided attitude.
Summarizing Ryder's biography and possessions without analyzing what the details suggest about respectability and race.
Bringing in plot events or author biography not found in the passage instead of analyzing the given text.
Missing the shift in the passage from the collective satire of the society to the individual, more sympathetic portrait of Ryder.

samples.essay:
In the opening of "The Wife of His Youth," Chesnutt's narrator sounds a lot like a member of the club he is describing. He is courteous and measured, and he never quite accuses anyone of anything. That politeness is the joke. Through hedging syntax, denials that end up confirming what they deny, and a portrait of Mr. Ryder built out of concessions and inventories, the narrator gives the Blue Veins real credit for their ambition and refinement while letting their color prejudice show through the gaps in their own explanations. The irony stays quiet because it borrows the society's genteel manner, so the style ends up taking part in the respectability it questions.

The narrator's treatment of the society as a group depends on qualifiers. The members are light-skinned "By accident, combined perhaps with some natural affinity," a phrase that pretends to be neutral but slips. "By accident" and "perhaps" sound fair-minded, but "natural affinity" suggests that lightness is something the members are drawn to, a preference and not a coincidence. The nickname comes from "some envious outsider," which seems to dismiss it, yet it was "readily adopted," and a joke only spreads that fast if people think it is accurate. The society's official claim, that "character and culture were the only things considered," comes to us in indirect speech, so the narrator reports it without standing behind it. Still, he is not just mocking. The excuse that light-skinned people had "better opportunities" is partly true, given slavery's history, and the narrator lets it be both a plausible point and a convenient one.

The irony is sharpest with the critics who change sides once they get "on the inside." Their praise piles up into "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield," and the list is inflated past the point of meaning anything. Then the scriptural "pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night" turns a social club into the guide that led Israel out of Egypt. This exaggeration exposes how quickly principle gives way to belonging. But "the social wilderness" is not a totally empty phrase, because freed people after the war really were in an unfamiliar world. So the satire is aimed at the converts' zeal and not at the need the society answers. The same doubleness shows up in the sentence about free birth: "while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true" that few "would have been unable to meet it." The double negative and the long, winding clauses copy the society's own evasions. Even slavery gets edited, since "romantic circumstances" serve to "rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects." Painful history is rewritten as respectable romance, and the narrator's mild word "grosser" makes the cover-up sound like good taste.

Mr. Ryder gets a warmer but still ironic portrait. The language of office, "custodian of its standards, and the preserver of its traditions," honors his leadership, and the image of him fanning "the embers until they burst again into a cheerful flame" is honestly affectionate. Yet just before this the narrator calls him "one of the most conservative" about "the things they collectively disclaimed," so the standards he guards include the prejudice the group denies. The list of his traits makes this concrete: "his hair was almost straight" sits in the same series as "his morals above suspicion," and the parallel syntax treats nearness to whiteness as if it were a virtue. The word "almost" measures him on the same scale the society pretends it doesn't use. His rise from messenger to stationery clerk is real self-made success, though the grand phrasing about supplies "for the whole company" gently deflates it. The concession "if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty" leads into a soul that "disarmed criticism," and the narrator seems disarmed too. Even his "very comfortable house on a respectable street," with its piano and engravings, measures worth in objects.

The last sentence turns from public standards to private desire, as Molly Dixon makes Ryder want to "change his condition." That word echoes the "social condition" the society was founded to improve. It hints that Ryder's carefully guarded standards are about to meet his personal life, and that the narrator's balance of respect and irony is going to be tested along with them.

annotations.comment: Analyzes syntax as a technique and connects it to the claim about denials that admit what they deny.

annotations.comment: Explains how the list structure ties Ryder's 'distinction' to color. Together with the metaphor, allusion, and concession analysis, this shows multiple techniques building meaning across the passage, which supports a 4.

annotations.comment: Opens a complex argument that the narrator's genteel voice is the tool of the satire. The essay returns to this idea with the mild word 'grosser' and the narrator being 'disarmed,' so it is sustained.

annotations.comment: Works through the tension instead of settling into pure mockery, treating the society's purpose as legitimate even while exposing it.

In this passage from "The Wife of His Youth," Charles Chesnutt's narrator describes the Blue Vein Society and Mr. Ryder with a tone that is respectful on the surface but quietly ironic underneath. The narrator admires the ambition and self-improvement of these people, but he also shows, through careful wording, that their claims about "character and culture" hide a prejudice about color and class that they will not admit.

The irony is clearest in how the narrator describes the society's rules. The society "did not allow that any such requirement existed," yet the narrator notes that most members were "more white than black." The narrator never directly accuses them, but by putting the denial next to the fact, the reader sees the contradiction. The same thing happens with free birth. The narrator says "there was really no such requirement," and then adds that "very few of the members" would have failed it anyway. The hedging words like "doubtless" and "generally speaking" make the narrator sound polite and fair, but they actually admit the thing the Blue Veins deny. The narrator also uses the critics who first attacked the society as "prejudice" and then, once inside, called it "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield." The long list of metaphors is exaggerated, and the biblical "pillar of cloud" makes the society sound almost holy. This shows the narrator smiling at how people change their opinion when they benefit.

Toward Mr. Ryder the tone is warmer, though still not simple. The narrator gives a lot of specific detail about his success: he rose from messenger to stationery clerk, saved money, owned a "comfortable house," and had a library and a piano. These details show real respect, because Ryder worked for what he has. The sentence about his poetry is a good example of the mixed attitude. His "pronunciation was sometimes faulty," but his gestures "disarmed criticism." The narrator admits a flaw and then forgives it, which suggests sympathy for Ryder's sincere love of poetry. However, the narrator also says Ryder's appearance "confer[s] distinction" on the Blue Veins and mentions that "his hair was almost straight." Here Ryder's value to the society is tied to how close he is to white, which brings the irony back in. Calling him "dean" and "custodian of its standards" also makes him sound like an official guarding something, and the narrator says he was "one of the most conservative."

The passage ends by turning to Mrs. Molly Dixon, which hints that Ryder's life is not as controlled as he thinks. Overall, the narrator respects the Blue Veins and Ryder for their effort, but uses polite, hedged language to show that their standards are less open than they say.

annotations.comment: Recognizes the concessive structure and links it to sympathy, showing how the attitude is divided in Ryder's portrait.

annotations.comment: Begins to hold respect and irony together in one figure, but this tension is not sustained or developed, so it falls short of real sophistication.

annotations.comment: Brief speculation about the ending with little textual grounding; a passing remark rather than a sustained complex argument.

In this passage Charles Chesnutt describes the Blue Vein Society and Mr. Ryder. The narrator talks about how the society started and what kind of people were in it, and then he describes Mr. Ryder who is the leader. The narrator seems to respect them but also finds some things funny about them, and Chesnutt uses different literary techniques to show this.

At the start the narrator explains that the society was organized "shortly after the war" to set up "correct social standards." This shows the society had a good purpose because the people needed improvement. But then the narrator says that the members were "more white than black," which shows that the society was really about color. The Blue Veins say that "character and culture" were the only things considered, but the narrator does not seem to believe this. He uses a kind of irony because he says one thing but the reader knows it is different.

Later the narrator talks about critics who attacked the society and then got in and called it "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield." This is a list which is exaggerated and it makes the critics seem like hypocrites. The narrator is making fun of them a little.

When the narrator describes Mr. Ryder he is mostly positive. Ryder worked his way up from messenger to stationery clerk, and he reads poetry and owns a nice house. These details show he is a hard worker and self-made. The narrator says "his hair was almost straight" which shows that looks matter to the Blue Veins too. Ryder is also called "one of the most conservative" so he is strict about the rules.

In conclusion, Chesnutt uses irony, lists, and details about Ryder to show that the narrator respects the Blue Veins but also sees their prejudice. The passage ends with Mrs. Molly Dixon, which sets up the rest of the story.

annotations.quote: The narrator does not seem to believe this.
annotations.comment: The essay quotes 'character and culture' but never explains how the narrator's wording, such as the hedged denials, creates the doubt. The commentary is a bare assertion.

annotations.quote: He uses a kind of irony because he says one thing but the reader knows it is different.
annotations.comment: This names irony and defines it generally without showing how the passage's syntax or diction produces it. Evidence is present but the explanation is thin.

annotations.comment: This is a relevant observation about the inflated metaphors. It is a start at technique analysis, but it does not note the scriptural allusion or the critics' change of mind once 'on the inside'.

annotations.quote: These details show he is a hard worker and self-made.
annotations.comment: The essay mostly paraphrases Ryder's career and possessions. It does not explain how they measure respectability or how the narrator's tone is both admiring and ironic.

blueprint.central_idea: Through a courteous, measured narrative voice, the passage both honors and gently satirizes a post-war society of light-skinned colored people and its leader, Mr. Ryder: it respects their ambition and self-made refinement while exposing, through hedged denials and inflated praise, the color and class prejudice they officially disclaim.
blueprint.complexity: The irony works through restraint, not open attack. The narrator borrows the society's own genteel style to show its contradictions, and the respect for Ryder is real even as his distinction is tied to near-white features and guarding exclusive standards. Students have to hold sympathy and critique together, notice the shift from group satire to individual portrait, and see how the ending turns toward personal desire.
